other_side: Where McCrory reads a stable labour market and rising productivity as proof that AI is a real, value-creating technology quietly augmenting workers, Zitron denies the premise underneath it: that AI is producing measurable economic value at all. He argues the AI build-out "isn't a result of any actual return on investment — whether that be in purely monetary terms, like revenue or profitability, productivity gains, or anything tangible or measurable," but is instead "the greatest capital misallocation in history," held aloft only because OpenAI has not yet collapsed. On his reading, the very productivity figures McCrory cites are noise dressed up as signal; the honest test is not the unemployment rate but whether the trillions in spending ever convert into durable profit, and he expects they will not.
truth_beneath: The single variable both men orbit is whether AI is yet producing real, measurable economic value — the productivity that McCrory says is already visible and Zitron says does not exist. Both accept the plain facts: unemployment sits near 4.2%, no mass AI layoffs have arrived, and capital spending is enormous. The empirical question that will resolve is whether the recent uptick in labour productivity (2% versus 1.6% before the pandemic) is genuinely AI-driven and durable, or a transient blip; the observable that settles it is sustained total-factor productivity growth attributable to AI alongside real firm-level returns, set against whether OpenAI's finances and remaining performance obligations actually hold. The residue is worldview: McCrory reads early numbers as augmentation beginning to show; Zitron reads the same spending as psychosis awaiting its Lehman moment. McCrory is vindicated if productivity growth persists and firms bank real returns without a lab collapsing; Zitron if the gains revert and OpenAI's funding unravels. Both are polemicists with incentives — NLW bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype — so the signal is where they agree despite opposite priors: both concede AI has not yet produced mass unemployment. Watch the next few quarters of aggregate productivity data, and whether OpenAI's committed spending stays funded.
